title: The distribution of weekly earnings of full-time employees
text:
In this exercise, you can recreate ONS labour market analysis reported in the table EARN04: Gross weekly earnings of full-time employees ### https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/datasets/grossweeklyearningsoffulltimeemployeesearn04 [last accessed 24/04/2021]. Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using the Quarterly Labour Force Survey.
Learning outcomes:

To become more familiar with the QLFS for earnings analysis, including key variables and appropriate use of the income weight.



The data used relates to an estimate for Oct-December 2020. To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2020.



Once you have downloaded the data, save it some where accessible.
library(haven) 
library(tidyverse)
library (sjmisc) #used for some of the tables 

#Open data and keep relevant variables.
lfs_od20 <- haven::read_dta("~/Data/lfs/UKDA-8777-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od20_eul_pwt24.dta")
As the dataset is large, let’s save a copy with just the variables we will use.
dataex2 <- lfs_od20 %>% select(PERSNO, PWT24, PIWT24, GRSSWK, INECAC05, FTPT, HOURPAY, SEX)###

QuestionAnswer


*Move this lower?
Why do we use a different weight from exercise 1?









To start, we will select only those in fulltime employment with valid income values. Replace the * in the code below with the correct values.
##replace the * to complete the code. 

md <- filter(dataex2, (PIWT24>0) & (HOURPAY>=0 & HOURPAY<=100) & (FTPT==* | FTPT==*) & (INECAC05==*) & is.na(GRSSWK)==FALSE)
Note - you can use the code below to check values and value labels for variables.
head(dataex2$INECAC05) head(dataex2$FTPT)

QuestionAnswer


What is the complete code?









Use the code below to recreate the ONS results showing the distribution of income for fulltime employees, overall and by sex.
md %\>% uncount(weights = .\$PIWT24) %\>% summarise(Median=median(GRSSWK))md %\>% uncount(weights = .\$PIWT24) %\>% group_by(SEX) %\>% summarise(Mean=mean(GRSSWK))md %\>% uncount(weights = .\$PIWT24) %\>% group_by(SEX) %\>% summarise(Median=median(GRSSWK))LFS_design \<- md %\>% as_survey_design(weights = PIWT24)LFS_design %\>% group_by(SEX) %\>% srvyr::summarise(survey_old_quantile(GRSSWK, c(.1,.25,.5,.75,.9)))

\## NOTE: Note that the behavior of the quantile functions has changed in srvyr version 1.1, but the old functions are still (currently) supported as survey_old_quantile and survey_old_median if you need to replicate the old results (as seen here). For more details about what has changed, see Thomas Lumley's blog post on the changes, available here: \<https://notstatschat.rbind.io/2021/07/20/what-s-new-in-the-survey-package/\>## An example of the quantile function can be found on CRAN: \<https://rdrr.io/cran/srvyr/man/survey_quantile.html\>

QuestionAnswers


What are median weekly earnings?
What are earnings at the lowest decile for males and females?









Note to self - Add code to get total if not produced by the code used above. LFS_design %>% summarise(survey_total())

QuestionAnswer


The ONS table gives the estimated number of full-time employees as 21,215,000. Above, we get 21,138,049. Why is there a difference?
What steps above need to be different to get the correct estimate of the number of full-time employees?

Move to the next exercise, which uses one of the longitudinal data sets.

title: Estimates of temporary employment
text:
In this exercise, we will recreate ONS labour market analysis published online in the table EMP07 Temporary Employees. Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using the Quarterly Labour Force Survey (QLFS).
Learning outcomes:

To become more familiar with QLFS datasets.
To become familiar with producing weighted population estimates
To understand how some ONS estimates are produced



The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for July-September 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, July - September, 2024.



One you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible, for example in a folder named LFS_exercises. We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let’s load the packages that are are going to need:

library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(survey)
library(srvyr)


## #setwd ("~/LFS_exercises")


# Inport  the data from a Stata format dataset
lfs_js24 <- read_dta("lfsp_js24_eul_pwt24.dta")

Inspect the dataset and find out the number of cases and variables.

ncol(lfs_js24) # Number of columns

[1] 767

nrow(lfs_js24) # Number of rows (observations)

[1] 59139

dim(lfs_js24)  # Both

[1] 59139   767



QuestionsAnswers



How many variables are there?




767




As there are many variables in the dataset, let’s create a copy with just the variables we will use. We can also use this opportunity to make the variable categories easier to understand by converting them into factors. For greater clarity, we also remove unused categories of categorical variables using droplevels().

mydata <- lfs_js24 |> 
  select(PERSNO, PWT24, JBTP101, FTPT, INECAC05, JOBTYP, SEX)|>
  mutate(across(.cols=JBTP101:SEX, 
                .fns=as_factor,"both")
         )|>
  droplevels()




We can have a look at the raw data by using head() or View()

head(mydata)

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  PERSNO    PWT24 JBTP101             FTPT                INECAC05  JOBTYP SEX  
  <dbl+lbl> <dbl> <fct>               <fct>               <fct>     <fct>  <fct>
1 1           631 [-9] Does not apply [-9] Does not apply [31] Ina… [-9] … [2] …
2 2             0 [-9] Does not apply [-9] Does not apply [31] Ina… [-9] … [1] …
3 1           701 [-9] Does not apply [-9] Does not apply [31] Ina… [-9] … [2] …
4 2           911 [-9] Does not apply [1] Full time       [2] Self… [-9] … [1] …
5 1           591 [-9] Does not apply [-9] Does not apply [31] Ina… [-9] … [2] …
6 1           901 [-9] Does not apply [-9] Does not apply [31] Ina… [-9] … [2] …

View(mydata) # A nicer looking output

Now let’s examine all variables in more detail.

mydata |> select(JBTP101, FTPT, INECAC05, JOBTYP, SEX) |> 
           summary()

                                       JBTP101                       FTPT      
 [-9] Does not apply                       :57940   [-9] Does not apply:30297  
 [-8] No answer                            :    2   [-8] No answer     :   31  
 [1] Working for an employment agency      :  185   [1] Full time      :21040  
 [2] Casual work                           :  291   [2] Part time      : 7767  
 [3] Seasonal work                         :   72   [3] New Deal-FT    :    2  
 [4] Under contract for a fixed period/task:  484   [4] New Deal-PT    :    2  
 [5] Other reason                          :  165                              
                                                             INECAC05    
 [1] Employee                                                    :24635  
 [31] Inactive, not seeking, not like, retired from paid work    :11694  
 [34] Under 16                                                   :10657  
 [2] Self-employed                                               : 4080  
 [27] Inactive, not seeking, not like, long term sick or disabled: 1997  
 [24] Inactive, not seeking, not like, student                   : 1381  
 (Other)                                                         : 4695  
                           JOBTYP              SEX       
 [-9] Does not apply          :34496   [1] Male  :28622  
 [-8] No answer               :   17   [2] Female:30517  
 [1] Permanent                :23427                     
 [2] Not permanent in some way: 1199                     
                                                         
                                                         
                                                         


We can also inspect the description of a variable by looking at its label. Let’s take for example FTPT:

attr(lfs_js24$FTPT,"label")

[1] "Whether working Full or Part Time"


A common way of getting frequency tables in R consists in using table():

t<-table(mydata$FTPT) ### Simple frequency table

t


[-9] Does not apply      [-8] No answer       [1] Full time       [2] Part time 
              30297                  31               21040                7767 
    [3] New Deal-FT     [4] New Deal-PT 
                  2                   2 


We can also examine percentages:

t<- 100*prop.table(t) ### Getting percentage
t


[-9] Does not apply      [-8] No answer       [1] Full time       [2] Part time 
       51.230152691         0.052418878        35.577199479        13.133465226 
    [3] New Deal-FT     [4] New Deal-PT 
        0.003381863         0.003381863 


Finally we can round the percentages in order to make them easier to read:

t<-round(t,1) ### Rounding to one digit

t


[-9] Does not apply      [-8] No answer       [1] Full time       [2] Part time 
               51.2                 0.1                35.6                13.1 
    [3] New Deal-FT     [4] New Deal-PT 
                0.0                 0.0 



QuestionsAnswers



How many cases are there?
What does the variable INECAC05 relate to?
Why are there many missing cases on the variables: JBTP101, FTPT and JOBTYP.




There are 59,139 cases
INECAC05 records NULL
Respondents not in employment are coded as missing values for these variables.




Missing values were recorded as -9 “Does not apply” and -8 “No answer” in the original data.



In order to provide reliable estimates of population values, survey data needs to be weighted when analysed. Weights are variables whose values increase or decrease the relative importance of observations, depending on how likely respondents were to take part to the survey. Some weights are only designed to correct the relative importance of observations, whereas others in addition also enable calculating population totals - the latter are called grossing weights.
Below, we compare weighted and unweighted frequencies and percentages again.
We will be using as_survey_design(), a R function from the survey and srvyr packages that in effect creates a weighted version of our data.
Let us first examine the variable measuring - JOBTYP - whether respondents work in a temporary job or not:

table(mydata$JOBTYP)


          [-9] Does not apply                [-8] No answer 
                        34496                            17 
                [1] Permanent [2] Not permanent in some way 
                        23427                          1199 

round(100*prop.table(table(mydata$JOBTYP)),1)


          [-9] Does not apply                [-8] No answer 
                         58.3                           0.0 
                [1] Permanent [2] Not permanent in some way 
                         39.6                           2.0 


… and create a version without missing values.

mydata <- mydata |> 
                  mutate (
                     JobTmp = ifelse(JOBTYP == "[2] Not permanent in some way",
                                      "Temporary",
                                      "Not temporary"),
                     JobTmp = ifelse(JOBTYP == "[-9] Does not apply" | JOBTYP == "[-8] No answer",
                                      NA,
                                      JobTmp),
                    JobTmp = as.factor(JobTmp)
                  )

table(mydata$JobTmp)


Not temporary     Temporary 
        23427          1199 


Using a function from the survey package, we create a weights-aware version of the data that we will be using for susbsequent analysis:

mydata.s<-mydata|> 
         filter(!is.na(PWT24) ) |> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)

Please note that we needed to remove observations with missing weights values, in effect observations that should not be taken into account to calculate population values. If we don’t we will get an error message.
We can now compute weighted frequencies and percentages using a survey specific command: svytable():

svytable(~JobTmp, mydata.s)

JobTmp
Not temporary     Temporary 
     27710056       1563699 

round(100*
       prop.table(
         svytable(~JobTmp, mydata.s)
         ),1
      )

JobTmp
Not temporary     Temporary 
         94.7           5.3 





QuestionsAnswers



Do the frequencies change noticeably when the weight is applied?
Create a variable to indicate those working part time and examine weighted and unweighted frequencies.




PWT24 is a grossing weight. Therefore, frequencies now reflect population totals.
The syntax below computes a variable recording whether respondents work part-time or not and produce weighted frequency tables.


 mydata <- mydata |> 
                  mutate (
                    PartTime = ifelse(FTPT == "[4] New Deal-PT" | FTPT  == "[2] Part time",
                                      "Part-time",
                                      "Not part-time"),
                   PartTime = ifelse(FTPT == "[-9] Does not apply" | FTPT == "[-8] No answer",
                                      NA,
                                      PartTime),

                    PartTime = as.factor(PartTime)
                  )


mydata.s<-mydata|> 
         filter(!is.na(PWT24) ) |> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)

round(100*
       prop.table(
         table(mydata$PartTime)
         ),1
      )


Not part-time     Part-time 
           73            27 

round(100*
       prop.table(
         svytable(~PartTime, mydata.s)
         ),1
      )

PartTime
Not part-time     Part-time 
         74.9          25.1 









It is straightforward to obtain the percentages of full-time and part-time employees by job tenure, by creating a contingency table:

t1<-svytable(~PartTime+JobTmp,mydata.s)

t1

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time      21628182    704932
  Part-time           6072026    855547

            round(
                  100*prop.table(
                   t1
                   ,1) # Requests denominators to be each working time status
                  ,1)

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time          96.8       3.2
  Part-time              87.7      12.3


We can add a third variable to the table to simultaneously examine the number of temporary and part-time employees by gender.

t2<-svytable(~PartTime+JobTmp+SEX,mydata.s)

            round(
                  100*prop.table(
                   t2
                   ,3) # Requests denominators to be each gender/working time combination.
                  ,1)

, , SEX = [1] Male

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time          84.8       2.8
  Part-time              10.0       2.4

, , SEX = [2] Female

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time          63.2       2.0
  Part-time              31.3       3.5





QuestionsAnswers



How many people are temporary employees (all and part-time) in this quarter?
How many females are in part-time temporary employment?
How many applicable cases to we have for the above analysis?




There are 1,563,699 temporary employees.
There are 509,693 females in part-time temporary employment
In order to get the number of valid cases, we need to look at unweighted frequencies. The number of (unweighted) valid cases for this analysis is 24,616




Note: You can check if your results match those in the ONS EMP07 dataset.

                                      PartTime),

                    PartTime = as.factor(PartTime)
                  )

title: Estimates of temporary employment
text:
It is straightforward to obtain the percentages of full-time and part-time employees by job tenure, by creating a contingency table:

t1<-svytable(~PartTime+JobTmp,mydata.s)
